paragraphs: While a character is under the effect of Critical Up (X), they reduce the value required to score a critical by X when making ability checks. Critical Up (X) enhancements can be stacked.

While a character is under the effect of Drain (X), their abilities restore X HP each time they deal damage. When using abilities that affect multiple targets or deal multiple instances of damage, HP is recovered for each target damaged or each instance of damage dealt. Drain cannot stack, and only the highest Drain is resolved when damage is dealt. Drain is removed at the end of the character’s turn.

While a character is under the effect of Revifify (X), they recover X HP at the end of the [Adventurer Step] or [Enemy Step], as determined by their standing relative to the player characters.

Revifify cannot stack, and only the highest Revifify is resolved each round. Should multiple effects need to be resolved simultaneously, the adventurers may decide the order in which to do so.

While a character is under the effect of Transcendent, they are immune to damage and enfeeblements inflicted by enemy abilities, traits, and encounter mechanics. Transcendent is removed at the start of the character's turn, or when the character uses an ability.

X Resistance (Y) is a temporary trait that prevents the user from being afflicted with the specified enfeeblement. When this character is afflicted with the X enfeeblement, that enfeeblement is immediately removed.

This trait is removed after being resolved Y times.
While a character is under the effect of X Ready, they may use an ability that requires them to be under the effect of this enhancement. X Ready is removed after the ability is used.

lists: While Bound, small and medium characters' Speed falls to 0, while larger characters' Speed is reduced by 2.
Characters receive one advantage die when making ability checks targeting a Bound enemy.
Bind is removed after a period of time specified by the effect that inflicted it elapses.

A Blinded character cannot see and automatically fails checks that rely entirely on vision. Ability checks made when using abilities that target enemies or allies incur a penalty listed below, as Blinded characters can still rely on their other senses to get a general idea of the target's position.
A Blinded character incurs a -2 penalty on all checks.
Characters receive one advantage die when making ability checks targeting a Blinded enemy.
A character on the Brink of Death incurrs a -5 penalty to all checks.
If a character on the Brink of Death is the target of another effect that inflicts Weakness, they are instead afflicted with Comatose.
Brink of Death does not wear off at the end of a phase, and can only be removed by completing a rest, or by effects that specifically remove it.
A Comatose character is treated as if they were Knocked Out for gameplay purposes.
Comatose can only be removed by spending one sun — a full day in-game — in a location where appropriate medical treatment is available, as determined by the GM.
A Comatose character has all other enhancements and enfeeblements removed. They cannot be granted any enhancements or afflicted with further enfeeblements other than Death.
Damage over time effects always specify the amount of damage they inflict using a set of parentheses, such as DOT (3) or DOT (User's INT).
An adventurer or ally afflicted with a damage over time effect takes damage specified by the DOT at the end of each round's [Adventurer Step].
An enemy afflicted with a damage over time effect takes damage specified by the DOT at the end of each round's [EnemyStep].
As the name implies, a Dead character has died and can no longer participate in the game.
Unless otherwise specified, Death cannot be reversed or removed.
Characters who have been Knocked Out or are Comatose will not Die, unless the scenario or the GM rules otherwise.
Characters that have been afflicted with Enmity incur a -5 penalty on all ability checks that do not target the character that inflicted it.
Enmity is removed at the end of the phase, at the end of the afflicted character’s turn, or when the character that inflicted it is Knocked Out.
A Heavy character has their Speed halved (rounded up, typically 3 squares) and cannot be affected by effects which would add to their Speed.
Ability checks targeting a Heavy character automatically result in direct hits.
Heavy is removed at the end of the Heavy character's turn, unless otherwise stated.
A character that has been Knocked Out is unconscious and cannot perceive their surroundings. They cannot use abilities or perform other actions during their turn.
A character that has been Knocked Out is treated as both Prone and Stunned.
A character that has been Knocked Out cannot recover HP or MP.
Knocked Out does not wear off at the end of a phase, and can only be removed by effects that specifically remove it.
A character that has been Knocked Out has all other enhancements and enfeeblements removed. They cannot be granted any enhancements or afflicted with further enfeeblements other than Comatose.

If a Paralyzed character uses a primary ability and rolls a 5 or lower for its ability check, Paralysis interrupts the ability, negating it completely. Do not resolve any of its effects, including its base effect. If the interrupted ability has a limited number of uses, none of its uses are consumed and the character may attempt to use the ability again on a later turn.
Paralysis is removed at the end of the Paralyzed creature's turn.
A Petrified character cannot act during their turn or use instant abilities.
Characters receive one advantage die when makingg ability checks targeting a Petrified enemy.
A Petrified character incurs a -5 penalty on all checks.
Petrify is removed at the end of the Petrified character's next turn.

A Prone character cannot take a standard movement on their turn less they spend half their Speed (rounded up, typically 3 squares) to get back on their feet. Standing up in this fashion removes Proney.
A Prone character incurs a -2 penalty on all checks.
Characters receive one advantage die when making ability checks targeting a Prone enemy.
Prone does not stack, even if it is inflicted multiple times. In these case, only a single instance of the effect remains.
A Silenced character cannot use invoked abilities.
Silence is removed at the end of the Silenced character's turn unless specified otherwise.
A Sleeping character incurs a -3 penalty on all checks.
Sleep is removed when a Sleeping character takes damage.
Characters may use a primary action to wake a Sleeping character in an adjacent square. Being roused in this fashion removed Sleep.
A Slowed character has their Speed halved (rounded up, typically 3 squares) and cannot be affected by effects which would add to their Speed.
A Slowed character incurs a -2 penalty on all checks.
A Stunned character cannot act during their turn or use instant abilities.
Any and all markers for which a Stunned character is the creator are removed.
Characters receive one advantage die when making ability checks targeting a Stunned enemy.
A Stunned character incurs a -5 penalty on all checks.
Stun can only be removed via the means detailed in the description of the effect that inflicted it. It cannot be removed by effects that remove enfeeblements.
A character that has been Stunned cannot be Stunned again in the same encounter.
A Weakened character incurs a -2 penalty on all checks.
If a character afflicted with Weakness is the target of another effect that inflicts this enfeeblement, they are instead afflicted with Brink of Death.
Weakness does not wear off at the end of a phase, and can only be removed by completing a rest or by effects that specifically remove it.

paragraphs: Strength — or STR — represents your adventurer’s athleticism, physical fitness, and the raw power they can bring to bear. This attribute is used when employing physical force to overcome a situation, such as lifting a boulder, pushing or pulling a laden cart, or kicking down a door.
Dexterity — or DEX — represents your adventurer’s coordination, agility, reflexes, and balance. This attribute is used when sneaking, performing precision tasks, or traversing narrow ledges.

Vitality — or VIT — represents your adventurer’s hardiness, physical health, and endurance. This attribute is used when holding one’s breath, performing manual labor for long periods of time, or attempting to survive in a desert without water.

Intelligence — or INT — represents your adventurer’s sharpness of mind, ability to recall information, and reasoning skills. This attribute is used when attempting to reach a logical conclusion, trying to remember a relevant fact, or searching for hidden objects.

Mind — or MND — represents your adventurer’s perceptiveness, instincts, and intuition. This attribute is used when discerning someone’s intent from their gestures, understanding how another person is feeling, noticing when something is out of place, or treating another character’s wounds.

Defense represents your adventurer’s ability to withstand physical forces.

This attribute is often used as the CR for the ability checks an enemy makes when attacking your adventurer with a physical ability.

Magic Defense represents your adventurer’s ability to withstand magical forces.

This attribute is often used as the CR for the ability checks an enemy makes when attacking your adventurer with a magic ability.
Speed represents the total number of squares your adventurer can move on their turn when performing a standard movement action.

Vigilance is a passive attribute that represents how aware your adventurer is of their surroundings at any given time.

This attribute is typically not used to make checks; rather, the GM will use an adventurer’s Vigilance to determine what they notice about their environment. Be sure to tell the GM your adventurer’s Vigilance when starting a new adventure.

Max HP determines how many hit points — or HP — your adventurer has. If their HP ever falls to zero, they lose consciousness and are unable to continue participating in an encounter.

As HP is not a measure of wellness or physique, an adventurer’s VIT does not influence their Max HP.
Max MP determines how many magic points — or MP — your adventurer has. Some abilities require adventurers to spend MP to use them. Unless otherwise stated, adventurers have a Max MP of 5.

When a character takes an action where the outcome is uncertain, the player controlling that character makes a check to determine success or failure.

To make a check, roll a d20 and add the appropriate value — usually a primary attribute. If this total equals or exceeds the check’s CR, your character succeeds. If the total is lower than the check’s CR, their attempt ends in failure.

Before making a check, the GM will determine the type of check required and assign it a CR.

d20 ＋ Value ＝ Total

Total ≧ CR ⇒ Success

Total ＜ CR ⇒ Failure

Some traits, abilities, enhancements, enfeeblements, and situations will grant you advantage dice or impose penalties when making certain checks.

Making Checks with Advantage Dice
Roll one extra d20 for each advantage die, then choose which result to use for the check. For example, if you have one advantage die when making a check, roll a total of two d20s, then choose which of the results to use.

Making Checks with Penalties
Subtract the largest applicable penalty from the total for the check.

Encounters play out over a series of rounds. Each round, all characters participating in the encounter take a single turn, beginning with the adventurers and their allies.

Encounter Overview

Starting an Encounter

  1. Surprise: The GM determines whether any of the characters participating in the encounter have been caught by surprise.

  2. Positioning: The GM determines the positions of all enemies participating in the encounter. Players do the same for their adventurers.

  3. Turn Order: Players determine the order in which their adventurers and allies take their turns.

Round Overview

  1. [Adventurer Step]: Each adventurer and allied character participating in the encounter takes a turn, following the turn order.

  2. [Enemy Step]: Each enemy participating in the encounter takes a turn.

  3. [End of Round Step]: The current round ends, a new round begins, and the order of play starts over at the [Adventurer Step].

Adventurer Turns Each turn, an adventurer can perform one of each of the following:

A Primary action

A Secondary Action

Standard Movement
or Focus

  • Primary Action: Use a primary or secondary ability.

  • Secondary Action: Use a secondary ability.

  • Standard Movement: Move a number of squares on the map up to your character’s Speed.

    Example: An adventurer with a Speed of five squares could move two squares, perform a primary action, move one square, perform a secondary action, then use the last two squares of their standard movement to move again before ending their turn.

  • Focus: Forgo all standard movement to perform an additional secondary action, for a total of two secondary actions in a single turn.

Instant Abilities: Instant abilities may be used during any character’s turn, provided their trigger conditions are met. However, a character cannot use multiple instant abilities on a given turn.

Some encounters consist of multiple phases. The start of a new phase may see enemy reinforcements take the field, or have a powerful foe adopt a new form.

When a phase ends and a new one begins, remove enhancements and enfeeblements from all characters. Adventurers with abilities that have limited uses per phase have those uses restored.

Turn order, HP, MP, barriers, items consumed, and benefits gained from traits are carried over to the new phase.

Ability Checks Many abilities require players to make an ability check when used during an encounter. These ability checks can have many purposes, but they are primarily used to determine if an ability scores a direct hit.

  • When using an ability with a check field, make an ability check using the indicated value. The ability check’s CR will be listed in the CR field, and is typically the target’s Defense or Magic Defense.
    If the ability check’s total is lower than the CR, simply resolve the ability’s base effect. If this total equals or exceeds the CR, resolve the effect described in its direct hit field as well.

  • When using an ability without a check field, simply resolve its base effect without making an ability check.

  • Criticals: If the d20 rolled for an ability check lands on a 20, that ability is a critical. Criticals double the number of dice rolled to determine the amount of damage dealt or HP healed by the ability’s effects.

  • Abilities with Multiple Targets: When using an ability that affects multiple targets, make a single ability check and use the resulting total to determine if the ability scores a direct hit on each target. If the ability deals damage or restores HP to multiple targets, roll the dice once. Each target suffers the same amount of damage or recovers the same amount of HP.

    If you have been granted advantage dice on ability checks against some targets but not others, roll the advantage dice for those targets separately.

During an encounter, the GM will inform players if and when limit breaks become available, after which the party can use up to three limit breaks. However, each adventurer can only use one limit break per encounter.
